title: The Stalk of Grass 10
content:
A flash of Bichen’s edge sliced clean across Xue Yang’s chest, splashing crimson into the mist. With the same fluid flick of the tip, the spirit-trapping pouch tucked inside his lapel was sent flying. Blinded by the swirling fog, Wei Wuxian called out, “Xue Yang! What did you want him to give back? Shuanghua? Shuanghua was never your sword. On what planet do you get to say ‘give it back’? Have some shame!”

Xue Yang burst into wild laughter. “Senior Wei, you really don't hold back, do you?”

“Laugh all you want,” Wei Wuxian said coldly. “Laugh until you drop dead—you still won't piece Xiao Xingchen’s soul back together. The man was thoroughly sickened by you, yet you’re still so desperate to drag him back to play house.”

Xue Yang veered wildly between hysterics and sudden fury. “Who the hell wants to play house with him?!”

“Then what were you doing on your knees, begging me to mend his soul?”

Xue Yang was far too sharp not to realize Wei Wuxian was intentionally rattling his cage—baiting him to slip up in anger and draw him into shouting so Lan Wangji could pinpoint his voice. Yet he couldn't stop the venom from pouring out. “What for? Ha! As if you don't know! I’m going to turn him into a fierce corpse, a vengeful spirit chained to my whim! He wanted to play the spotless saint, didn't he? I’ll make him butcher without end—never a single day of peace!”

Wei Wuxian countered, “Oh? You hate him that much? Then why did you kill Chang Ping?”

Xue Yang sneered. “Why did I kill Chang Ping? Is that even a question, Yiling Laozu? Didn't I tell you already? When I said I’d slaughter every living thing in the Yueyang Chang clan, I meant not even a stray dog would be spared!”

Every word out of his mouth was a flare pinpointing his position. The sickening thuds of steel biting into flesh came in rapid succession, yet Xue Yang’s pain tolerance bordered on demonic. Wei Wuxian had seen it firsthand through Empathy: even with a blade driven through his gut, the boy could carry on trading barbs with a smile.

Wei Wuxian pressed on, “Nice excuse, except the timeline is completely off. A vindictive snake like you—someone who repays a slight a thousandfold and leaves no loose ends—would never drag out a vendetta for years. Why you went back to murder Chang Ping, you know better than anyone.”

“Enlighten me, then!” Xue Yang’s voice cracked into a vicious snarl. “What do I know? What do I know?!”

“If all you wanted was his life, why execute him by lingchi—the punishment meant to atone for sin?” Wei Wuxian’s voice cut like a razor. “If you were taking revenge for yourself, why use Shuanghua instead of Jiangzai? And why gouge out Chang Ping’s eyes to make him match Xiao Xingchen?”

Xue Yang shrieked, beside himself with rage. “Bullshit! It’s all pure bullshit! It was revenge—did you expect me to give him a painless death?!”

“You were avenging someone,” Wei Wuxian retorted. “The question is: who were you actually avenging? It's pathetic. If you really wanted justice, the one who deserved to be carved into a thousand pieces was you!”

Two piercing whistles cut through the air. Wei Wuxian didn't flinch. In a blink, Wen Ning threw himself forward, swatting down a pair of skull-piercing nails dripping with foul resentful energy. A chilling, screeching chuckle—like an owl echoing through a graveyard—rippled through the fog, then cut off instantly. Xue Yang went dead silent, cutting his losses to focus entirely on Lan Wangji.

The bastard is cockroach-tough, Wei Wuxian thought, grim. Acts like pain doesn't exist, no matter how hard he’s hit. Just a couple more sentences and Lan Zhan would have carved him up. Too bad he’s finally wised up and clamped his mouth shut.

Right then, a crisp rhythm began tapping through the soup of fog. Clack. Clack. Clack.

A spark went off in Wei Wuxian’s mind. “Lan Zhan! Strike where the cane taps!”

Bichen flashed forward without a heartbeat's hesitation. A stifled grunt tore from Xue Yang's throat. Moments later, the rhythmic clatter sprang up yards away!

Lan Wangji’s blade followed the noise relentlessly. Xue Yang’s voice turned venomous: “Little blind brat, shadowing me like this… aren't you afraid I’ll crush you to dust?”

Ever since Xue Yang murdered her, A-Qing had spent years evading him in the shadows. For reasons unknown, Xue Yang had mostly ignored her wandering spirit, dismissing her as a harmless nuisance unworthy of his time. Yet here she was, clinging to his heel like a shadow in the heavy mist, slamming her bamboo pole into the stone to give away his position and guide Lan Wangji's lethal strikes!

Xue Yang shifted position at breakneck speed, darting across the street in the blink of an eye. But A-Qing had always been fleet on her feet in life; in death, she stuck to him like a curse, her cane hammering against the pavers in an unrelenting frenzy. The rapid tapping echoed near, then far, left, then right, impossible to shake off. And everywhere the sound landed, the icy glare of Bichen arrived an instant later!

Where Xue Yang had once owned the fog, striking from nowhere and vanishing at will, he was now forced to expend energy swatting at a ghost. Spitting a curse, he whipped his hand back, hurling an exorcism talisman behind him. In that split second of distraction, as A-Qing let out a shrill, eerie shriek, Bichen drove clean through his ribs!

Though the vicious talisman blew A-Qing’s spirit apart and silenced the tapping, the strike had landed flush in a vital spot. Xue Yang could no longer pull off his ghost-like evasion.

Ragged coughs wet with blood drifted through the mist. Wei Wuxian tossed an empty spirit-trapping pouch into the air, driving it to scoop up A-Qing’s scattered essence. A set of heavy, dragging footsteps stumbled forward, followed by a feral lunge. Xue Yang clawed outward with a raspy bellow: “Give it back!”

A brilliant streak of blue light flashed down. Clean and absolute, Lan Wangji severed his left arm.

Arterial crimson sprayed through the air, turning a massive patch of white vapor into a humid, rose-tinted haze. The stench of wet rust hung thick and heavy, but Wei Wuxian couldn't spare a glance; he was entirely consumed by gathering the remnants of A-Qing’s battered soul. Ahead, though Xue Yang never cried out in pain, the sickening thud of knees hitting cobblestones echoed through the quiet. Drained dry by the sheer volume of blood loss, his legs had finally given out.

Lan Wangji raised Bichen once more. The next strike would take his head.

Suddenly, a column of blue ghostfire flared through the fog, licking toward the sky.

A Transportation Talisman!

Knowing things had gone south, Wei Wuxian dashed forward, heedless of the danger. He nearly lost his footing on the slick stones; the ground was practically flooded with blood pooled from the severed arm.

Xue Yang, however, was gone.

Lan Wangji stepped out of the thinning mist. Wei Wuxian looked at him. “The gravedigger?”

Xue Yang was mortally wounded and missing an arm. Given the gruesome amount of blood soaking the stones, he was practically a corpse—he wouldn't have possessed the spiritual energy or mental focus to activate a high-tier transportation seal.

Lan Wangji gave a slight nod. “I struck the gravedigger three times. He could have been captured, but a horde of walking corpses intervened, allowing his escape.”

Wei Wuxian’s eyes darkened. “Even injured, he burned that much spiritual power just to drag Xue Yang’s body away. That means he knew who Xue Yang was—and what he carried. He took the body to search for the Yin Tiger Tally.”

Rumor had it that the Tally vanished without a trace after Jin Guangyao supposedly ‘disposed’ of Xue Yang. But seeing the sheer scale of the city, there was little doubt it had been on him all along. Yi City held thousands of poisoned living corpses, walking dead, and full-blown fierce corpses; crude corpse venom and skull-piercing nails weren't enough to manage that kind of army. The only thing capable of commanding them as a hive mind, hurling them forward without fear, was the Tiger Tally. A suspicious, paranoid snake like Xue Yang would never store something so dangerous out of arm’s reach—he needed it on his person where he could feel it at all times. Taking the body was as good as taking the Tally.

The gravity of it settled over them like lead. “At this point,” Wei Wuxian murmured, “we can only pray that whatever replica Xue Yang managed to patch together is severely limited in power.”

Lan Wangji tossed a small item across the space between them.

Wei Wuxian caught it on instinct. “What's this?”

“Right hand.”

It was a fresh Qiankun Pouch. The jolt reminded Wei Wuxian of their primary objective, and his spirits lifted slightly. “Our dear friend’s right hand?”

“Mn.”

Between fighting off the gravedigger, navigating the cursed fog, and cutting down swarms of dead, Lan Wangji had still managed to retrieve the missing limb. Wei Wuxian was genuinely impressed. “Leave it to Hanguang-jun! That puts us one step ahead again. Pity it wasn't the head—I was curious to see what our dear friend looked like, though I suppose we’ll find out soon enough… Wait, where’s Song Lan?”

With Xue Yang gone, the demonic mist had begun to pick up speed, thinning out enough to reveal the outlines of the street. It was only then that Wei Wuxian realized the fierce corpse had vanished. At the spot where he had fallen, only Wen Ning remained, squatting on the dirt and staring blankly in their direction.

Lan Wangji’s fingers rested against the hilt of his sheathed sword.

“It’s fine, lower your guard,” Wei Wuxian said quietly. “Song Lan doesn't have any fight left in him, otherwise Wen Ning would have raised an alarm. Now that his mind has cleared, he probably walked away on his own.”

He blew a soft, short whistle. Wen Ning rose with his head bowed, obediently melting back into the white fog until the heavy scrape of iron chains faded into the distance.

Lan Wangji offered no comment. “Let us go,” he said evenly.

They took a couple of steps before Wei Wuxian halted. “Hold on.”

Lying by itself in the crimson pool was a solitary object.

A severed left hand. Four fingers remained, curled tightly inward into a fist, the little finger missing entirely.

The grip was locked tight in rigor mortis. Wei Wuxian knelt, putting considerable muscle into prying each stiff finger open one by one. Nestled in the dead palm was a tiny piece of candy.

The sweet had darkened with dirt and age, long since unfit to eat.

Held with such desperate force for so long, it was already crushed to pieces.

Returning to the funeral hall, they found the front doors wide open. True to expectations, Song Lan stood beside Xiao Xingchen’s coffin, staring down at the still form resting within.

A flock of clan juniors huddled near the far wall, their swords drawn in white-knuckled terror as they watched the lethal fierce corpse that had nearly slaughtered them moments ago. When Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji stepped inside, the relief on their faces was palpable, though none dared make a sound for fear of provoking Song Lan.

Crossing the threshold, Wei Wuxian inclined his head toward Lan Wangji. “This is Daozhang Song Lan, Song Zichen.”

At the sound of footsteps, Song Lan turned his head. Lan Wangji gracefully lifted the hem of his robes, stepped over the high threshold, and offered a polite, solemn nod.

With his sanity restored, Song Lan’s irises had settled back into place, revealing dark, lucid pupils.

Those eyes had once belonged to Xiao Xingchen. And looking out from them now was a bottomless, unspeakable sorrow.

No one needed to ask. Wei Wuxian understood immediately: during all those years spent bound as a fierce corpse under Xue Yang’s thumb, he had seen every atrocity. He remembered every single moment.

To drag those memories into the light would only be pouring salt into the rawest of wounds.

After a heavy silence, Wei Wuxian pulled out two small, fragile spirit-trapping pouches and presented them with both hands. “Daozhang Xiao Xingchen. And Miss A-Qing.”

Terrified as A-Qing had been of Xue Yang, she had still clung to her killer's heels through the mist, keeping him pinned until Bichen ran him through. But Xue Yang’s parting talisman had nearly blasted her essence into oblivion. Wei Wuxian had scrambled with everything he had just to scoop up what little remained. Now, her soul was as fractured and spent as Xiao Xingchen’s.

Two pale, flickering wisps lay curled inside the small fabric bags, looking as though the slightest jostle might scatter them to the wind. Hands trembling, Song Lan received them, cradling the pouches flat against his palms. He didn't even dare hold them by the cords, terrified of the faintest sway.

“Daozhang Song,” Wei Wuxian asked gently, “what will you do with Daozhang Xiao Xingchen’s body?”

Keeping the pouches carefully braced in one hand, Song Lan drew Fuxue with the other. Using the tip of the blade, he carved two clean lines into the stone floor:

Cremate the remains. Nurture the souls.

Xiao Xingchen’s soul was shattered beyond repair; returning to a mortal vessel was out of the question, making cremation the gentlest end. Once the flesh turned to ash, the pure remnants of his spirit could slowly recover in peace. Perhaps, after years or centuries, he might walk the earth again.

Wei Wuxian nodded. “And where will you go from here?”

Song Lan carved again: Carry Shuanghua. Walk the mortal path. Slay evil beside Xingchen.

He paused, then added: When he wakes, tell him: ‘I am sorry. It was never your fault.’

Those were the words he never had the chance to say in life.

The demonic fog clinging to Yi City had begun to unravel, exposing the long streets and crossroads to the dull sky. Lan Wangji and Wei Wuxian led the junior cultivators through the gates of the abandoned ghost town. There, at the threshold, Song Lan took his leave.

Still clad in his ink-black Daoist robes, solitary as ever, he carried two swords across his back—Shuanghua and Fuxue—and guarded two fragile souls, Xiao Xingchen and A-Qing. He turned down a different path than the one that had led them into the valley.

Not the road back to the living world, but a lonely road of his own.

Lan Sizhui watched the retreating figure, murmuring softly, “‘The bright moon and gentle breeze, Xiao Xingchen; the proud snow and biting frost, Song Zichen’… I wonder if they will ever meet again.”

Wei Wuxian glanced down at the overgrown weeds by the trail, catching sight of a patch of wild grass. Back then, he thought, this was the very spot where Xiao Xingchen and A-Qing pulled Xue Yang out of the ditch.

Lan Jingyi broke the silence, bursting with curiosity. “Are you finally going to tell us what you saw in the Empathy trance? How was that guy Xue Yang? Why was he pretending to be Xiao Xingchen?”

“Yeah, and what about the Ghost General? Where did he go? Why didn't we see him leave? Is he still in the city? Why did he show up out of nowhere?!”

Conveniently ignoring the second volley of questions, Wei Wuxian cleared his throat. “Well, that’s quite a long and messy story…”

By the time the full tale was told, a heavy gloom hung over the entire group. Not a single person remembered to ask about the Ghost General.

Lan Jingyi was the first to dissolve into messy sobs. “How could something so awful happen in this world?!”

Jin Ling was vibrating with fury. “That scumbag Xue Yang! Filth! Dying like that was too easy on him! If Fairy were here, I’d have her tear him to pieces!”

Wei Wuxian shuddered inwardly: If Fairy were here, I’d have dropped dead of fright long before the dog could even touch Xue Yang.

The boy who had peeked through the door crack earlier clutched his chest in agony. “Miss A-Qing… poor Miss A-Qing!”

Lan Jingyi was bawling at the top of his lungs, completely discarding the Gusu Lan clan rules on composure, but no one bothered to scold him. Lan Sizhui’s eyes were rimmed in red as well, and Lan Wangji showed no intention of slapping a Silence Spell on them. Wiping snot and tears across his sleeve, Lan Jingyi choked out an idea: “Should we burn some joss paper for Daozhang Xiao Xingchen and Miss A-Qing? There’s a village near the crossroads ahead, right? Let’s buy some offerings to pay our respects.”

The boys chimed in immediately. “Yes! Let’s do that!”

Chatting along the way, they soon reached the village near the stone boundary marker. Lan Jingyi and Lan Sizhui practically bolted inside, snapping up a haphazard haul of joss sticks, white candles, and reams of yellow and red spirit money. Pulling off to the side of the road, they hastily cobbled together a makeshift windbreak out of loose mud-bricks and river stones. In no time at all, the entire flock of young cultivators dropped into a tight huddle around it on the dirt, torching the paper offerings while muttering a relentless stream of whispered prayers.

Wei Wuxian’s own mood hadn't been particularly stellar—he’d barely cracked a couple of jokes the entire hike back—but seeing this spectacle was the final straw. He leaned toward Lan Wangji, gesturing at the kids. "Hanguang-jun, you seeing this? They’re staging a whole roadside vigil right in front of someone’s front door. You really not going to rein them in?"

Lan Wangji’s reply was characteristically flat. "Go rein them in yourself."

"Fine," Wei Wuxian said. "I’ll do your parenting for you."

He sauntered over to the circle. "Am I seeing things? Aren't you all proper disciples from prominent, upright cultivation clans? Did your parents and clan elders completely skip the lesson about how the dead can’t cash paper money? When a person is dead and gone, what the hell are they going to spend coin on? It never reaches them. Not to mention you're parked right on someone's doorstep, burning—"

Lan Jingyi waved an arm at him dismissively. "Shoo, shoo! You're blocking the wind! It's going to go out! Besides, it's not like you've ever died before—how would you know whether the dead receive it or not?"

Beside him, another disciple lifted a soot-stained face streaked with muddy tear-tracks and chimed in, "Exactly! How would you know? What if it actually works?"

Wei Wuxian froze. "How would I know?"

How would I know?!

Because I was dead for over a decade, and I didn't see a single copper of it!

Before he could process the existential insult, Lan Jingyi drove the knife right between his ribs: "Even if you never got any, it's obviously because nobody gave enough of a damn to burn some for you."

Wei Wuxian's internal monologue screeched to a halt. No way. Am I really that big of a failure? Not one person in the entire world cared enough to burn me a single sheet of spirit money? Could that actually be why I never got anything?

The thought refused to sit right. Glancing back over his shoulder, he leaned in and lowered his voice toward Lan Wangji: "Hanguang-jun, be honest... Did you ever burn spirit money for me? At the very least, you had to have sent me something, right?"

Lan Wangji glanced at him, lowered his gaze to brush a stray speck of paper ash from the hem of his sleeve, and then silently looked out into the distance, offering not a single syllable.

Wei Wuxian stared at his serene profile, his heart sinking into his boots. You've got to be kidding me.

He really didn't?!

Before he could spiral any further, an aggrieved local farmer carrying a crude hunting bow tramped up the path, scowling at the smoke. "Hey! What do you kids think you're doing burning that junk right here? This is my front gate—it's bad luck, you hear me!"

Wei Wuxian smirked, nodding at the circle. "See? Told you so. Now you're getting an earful."

The sheltered disciples had never done anything like this before, completely oblivious to the local taboo against burning funeral money on someone else’s property, and scrambled to stammer out apologies. Lan Sizhui hastily wiped his grimy cheeks and stood up. "Is this your home, Uncle?"

The villager sneered, "What kind of foolish question is that? My family has lived on this patch of dirt for three generations! If it's not my home, is it yours?"

Jin Ling’s temper flared at the peasant's tone. He jumped to his feet, hand twitching toward his waist. "Watch your mouth! Who do you think—"

Wei Wuxian planted a firm palm directly onto Jin Ling's crown, shoving his head straight back down into a squat.

Lan Sizhui smoothed things over immediately. "I see. My apologies, I meant no disrespect. It's just that the last time we passed through this hamlet, we spoke with a different hunter sitting right here. That was the only reason I asked."

The villager blinked in total confusion. "A different hunter? What other hunter?"

He held up three stubby fingers. "Three generations of only sons! It's just me—no brothers! My old man's been in the dirt for years, and I haven't even taken a wife, let alone fathered a boy! Where the hell would another hunter crawl out from?"

Lan Jingyi scrambled to his feet to back Sizhui up. "There really was one!" he insisted. "He was bundled up tight with a massive conical hat pulled low over his face, sitting right there in your courtyard stringing a bow like he was gearing up for a hunt! When we got here, we asked him for directions, and he was the one who pointed us toward Yi City!"

The villager spat hard onto the dirt. "Bullshit! You're telling me you saw a guy sitting in my yard?! There's no one like that here! That dead-end corner of Yi City has ghosts vicious enough to skin a man alive—pointing you down that road? Whoever did that was trying to get you killed! You saw a damn ghost, that's what!"

He spat three more times to ward off the bad omen, shook his head in disgust, and marched off, leaving the disciples exchanging uneasy, wide-eyed stares in the rising smoke.

Lan Jingyi tried to justify himself, flustered: "He really was sitting right in that yard, I swear! I remember it clear as day..."

Wei Wuxian leaned in to murmur a few quick words to Lan Wangji before turning back to the group. "Starting to put the pieces together? You were baited into Yi City from the start. That 'hunter' who gave you directions wasn't a local at all—it was someone playing a part, setting you up."

Jin Ling’s eyes narrowed. "You mean the dead cats... From the very beginning, someone was deliberately leaving a trail of carcasses to lure us here? That fake hunter was the one doing it?"

"Ten to one, yeah."

Lan Sizhui furrowed his brow, deeply unsettled. "Why go through so much trouble just to drag us to Yi City?"

"Hard to say right now, but you need to keep your heads on a swivel from here on out," Wei Wuxian warned, his tone unusually firm. "If you run into anything this bizarre again, don’t play the brave hero and investigate it alone. Flare your clans, muster reinforcements, and move in numbers. If Hanguang-jun hadn't happened to be in Yi City this time, not one of you would have made it out alive."

The reality of that close call sent an icy prickle of dread down their spines. Getting swallowed whole by an endless horde of walking corpses was bad enough, but staring down a living demon like Xue Yang was the stuff of nightmares.

With the warning sinking in, Lan Wangji and Wei Wuxian herded the young flock along the road, reaching the neighboring market town where they’d stabled their mounts just as dusk settled over the rooftops.

The avenues here were blazing with warm lantern light, packed with the lively chatter of hawkers and bustling evening crowds. A collective wave of relief washed over the kids—now this was a place for the living.

Wei Wuxian opened his arms wide toward the stables, calling out affectionately, "Little Apple!"

The spotted donkey responded with an enraged, ear-splitting bray. Almost instantly, a thunderous bark cut through the air, and Wei Wuxian bolted, practically throwing himself behind Lan Wangji’s back like a frightened shadow. Fairy came barreling out of the stalls, and within seconds, dog and donkey were locked in a standoff, baring their teeth and practically spitting venom at each other.

Lan Wangji glanced down, unbothered. "Tether them. Food first."

Still hauling Wei Wuxian—who was clinging to his robes like a limpet—Lan Wangji followed the inn’s server up the wooden stairs toward the second floor. Jin Ling and the other juniors moved to trail behind them, but Lan Wangji paused on the landing, throwing a quiet, unreadable glance over his shoulder.

Lan Sizhui caught the hint instantly, turning to herd the others back down. "Elders and juniors should take separate tables. We’ll stay on the ground floor."

Lan Wangji offered a subtle nod of approval and continued up the stairs with his usual cool detachment. Jin Ling lingered awkwardly on the steps, stuck in place, until Wei Wuxian peeked over Lan Wangji’s shoulder with a cheeky grin. "Separate seating for the grownups and the kids. Trust me, there are things up here you're better off not seeing."

Jin Ling sneered, crossing his arms. "As if I'd want to watch anyway!"

Lan Wangji instructed the tavern staff to set up a hearty spread for the disciples downstairs before booking a private booth on the second floor, where he and Wei Wuxian settled across from each other at a polished wooden table.

Wei Wuxian leaned forward, his elbows on the wood. "Hanguang-jun, take my advice on this: do not let the Lan Clan shoulder the fallout of Yi City all on your own. A ghost town of that scale will drain a monstrous amount of manpower, coin, and resources to properly cleanse and lay to rest. It's a massive headache. Besides, the Shu region isn't even under Gusu Lan's jurisdiction to begin with. Take a look at the roster of kids downstairs, see which prominent families they belong to, and send every single one of their sects an invoice. They need to pull their own weight."

"It can be considered," Lan Wangji murmured.

"You need to seriously consider it," Wei Wuxian pressed. "These clans love nothing more than swooping in to steal the glory when game is spotted, but the second real accountability is on the line, they dodge it like the plague. If you take the hit for them today, you'll only spoil them rotten; they won't appreciate your sect's noble selflessness, and the next time disaster strikes, they'll just expect Gusu to play the savior as a matter of course. That's just how the world works."

He paused for a beat, his tone softening with a touch of melancholy. "Still, it really was rotten luck. Yi City was far too remote, and worse, it lacked a single Watchtower. If one had been stationed out there, Jin Ling and Sizhui never would have blundered inside blind, and the spirits of Lady A-Qing and Daozhang Xiao Xingchen wouldn't have spent all these years trapped in the dark waiting to be brought to light."

The great cultivation clans, large and small, were scattered across the realm like a sea of stars, but they overwhelmingly staked their claims in bustling transport hubs, prosperous trade capitals, or lush spiritual mountains. Bleak, impoverished borderlands were completely passed over; no noble family was willing to station their disciples in the dirt, and seasoned rogue cultivators rarely wandered through such backwaters. Consequently, whenever evil spirits or dark creatures plagued those corners, the local commoners were left entirely defenseless, trapped in misery with nowhere to turn for help.

Back when Jin Guangshan was still the Clan Leader of the Lanling Jin Sect, Jin Guangyao had proposed a sweeping reform to address this gap. But given the staggering costs involved, Jin Guangshan had shown zero enthusiasm for the project. Coupled with the fact that Lanling Jin didn't command enough absolute authority across the sects at the time, the proposal had been quietly shelved and forgotten.

Once Jin Guangyao formally took the reins as Clan Leader and ascended to the seat of Chief Cultivator, he immediately began pooling manpower and material resources across all clans to revive his vision. The initial pushback had been deafening; countless factions openly accused the Jin Clan of using the project as a pretext to line their own pockets and exert political control. Yet Jin Guangyao, wearing his signature polite smile, spent five grueling years grinding down the opposition. In those five years, he forged countless alliances, burned countless bridges, played both the carrot and the stick, and exhausted every dirty and clean trick in his arsenal until he brute-forced the initiative across the finish line—ultimately erecting over twelve hundred Watchtowers across the realm.

These Watchtowers were peppered throughout remote, impoverished territories, each permanently staffed by a rotation of disciples drawn from various sects. The moment abnormal resentful energy surfaced, the post would deploy immediately; if the threat proved beyond their depth, they would promptly launch an emergency flare to summon aid from nearby clans or wandering cultivators. And if the responding cultivators demanded a bounty that the destitute locals couldn't possibly afford, the annual defense fund raised by the Lanling Jin Sect was more than enough to foot the bill.

All of this had unfolded long after the Yiling Laozu was in the dirt. Passing a few of these garrisons during their recent travels, Wei Wuxian had only pieced together the full story after asking Lan Wangji about them. Word on the street was that Carp Tower was currently prepping the blueprints for a second wave of construction, aiming to expand the network to three thousand towers to blanket every blind spot on the map. Even though the first batch had proven its worth ten times over and won massive public acclaim, the skepticism and cynical jeers had never truly died down. When the expansion broke ground, it was guaranteed to kick up another monumental political storm.

Before long, the tavern hands bustled in, laying down a spread of steaming dishes alongside jars of local wine. Wei Wuxian cast a casual glance across the table—nearly two-thirds of the plates were glistening with fiery red chilies. He watched Lan Wangji’s chopsticks drift naturally toward the mild, pale dishes, only occasionally dipping into the crimson bowls, swallowing the blistering spice without so much as a flicker in his expression.

A quiet, strange warmth brushed against Wei Wuxian's ribs.

Catching the lingering stare, Lan Wangji paused, looking up. "What is it?"

Wei Wuxian reached out, slowly tilting the ceramic jug to pour himself a cup of wine.

"Nothing," he murmured, a faint, lopsided smile curling his lips. "Just... wishing I had someone to drink with."
